prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect

statement.case_for: I keep the topological-insulator case first. Kane and Mele turned a symmetry argument (time reversal, Kramers degeneracy, a Z2 invariant) into a concrete prediction of protected helical edge states, and Molenkamp's group then saw the predicted edge transport in HgTe/CdTe quantum wells. A prediction followed by a clean observation is the kind of discovery the prize is meant to honour. The idea is conceptually economical, it has been confirmed in several materials and by independent techniques over about two decades, and it reorganised how condensed-matter physicists classify band structures. It has the broadest opening support of any candidate on the shortlist: all eight members ranked it, five placed it in their top three and two placed it first. Recognition is not premature.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weak point. The HgTe proposal came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional topological insulators (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Roy, Hasan and others) are close to the boundary, so any trio leaves out people with real claims, and the committee would be framing the prize around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall state while a larger field is built on the 3D materials. Because no prize configuration can contain more than three people, a two-part prize that pairs this topic with anything else is in practice impossible, so choosing it is also a decision not to honour precision measurement or moire materials this year. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions also means some members may see the subject as already partly recognised.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first: Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's record performance, reproduced across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE and compared at the 1e-18 level, with the field mature and the credit a clean pair.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and maturity points; I ranked Katori and Ye third myself and treat B041 as my first alternative. Where I differ is on how much weight to give a possible redefinition of the second. The physics is established, but the committee should ask whether the decisive discovery is the lattice scheme itself or the later metrological performance, and whether the 2005 prize on frequency combs (Hall, Hansch) leaves less room. I put topological insulators ahead because the conceptual step, a new topological classification of matter, seems larger than an extension of precision metrology, though I accept that this is a judgement about scale and not about quality of work.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and places topological insulators sixth, noting that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Moore are unavailable, which leaves an attribution problem, while still calling the field mature and not premature.
responses.response: I share the attribution worry and it is my main reservation, but I do not think it lowers the case as far as a sixth place implies. The Kane-Mele prediction and the HgTe observation form a self-contained theory-plus-experiment story, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal sits between them as the route to the right material. A prize can credit the prediction and the observation without settling every sub-priority. I would also point out that circuit QED has the opposite difficulty, with four strong claimants (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin) for three places, and the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits makes its timing delicate. Those are not smaller problems than ours.

responses.point: Pearce ranks Halzen and IceCube first, as an instrument-driven discovery that opened neutrino astronomy, and accepts a one-name proposal as defensible while acknowledging the large collaboration and predecessors such as AMANDA.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube fifth and think it is a real discovery in the observational tradition. But I find a single name harder to defend than you do. If the discovery is the observation of the diffuse astrophysical flux, the committee has to explain why one person stands for a collaboration of hundreds, and what happens to the instrument leaders and the analysis that actually extracted the signal. A one-name prize is possible, as it would only use one of three places and could in principle sit beside another part, but I would want to see the attribution argument made explicitly. That uncertainty is part of why I ranked it fifth and do not carry it as an alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the twisted-bilayer-graphene case first: Bistritzer and MacDonald's 2011 flat-band prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity form a natural theory-plus-experiment prize, strongly confirmed by many groups, with timing that is mature enough yet still central; Mehlig ranks topological insulators second and calls them arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree that B030 has the same attractive structure as B018, prediction followed by observation, and I ranked it fourth, so it is my second alternative. My reservation is the one Eriksson and Olsson also raise: the origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated states is still debated, and the main experiments date only from 2018. A prize citation would have to describe what was discovered while the interpretation is open. Topological insulators have two decades of stable interpretation behind them. I would not argue the moire case is wrong, only that it is the better candidate in a few years, and that is the reason it sits behind B018 for me. If the committee weighs timing differently from me, I would not object to B030 as the lead.

uncertainties: Whether the citation should be framed around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect or around topological insulators generally, and which omissions that choice makes acceptable (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, and the 3D pioneers).
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions makes the committee see this topic as partly recognised.
How much weight to give the still-unsettled interpretation of the correlated and superconducting phases in twisted bilayer graphene, which decides whether B030 should overtake B018 now or later.
My knowledge of priority sequences among theory groups is from memory and is not independently verified here.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: my documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none of them is among the credited names of any shortlisted candidate.
